::: callout-outcomes

## 💡 Learning Outcomes

By the end of this module, learners will be able to:

- Select AI tools and approaches suited to different research tasks, evidence sources and data restrictions.
- Build reusable workflows with clear prompts, document context, iterative checks and records of decisions.
- Apply AI support across question development, theory, literature review, research design, analysis and academic writing.
- Verify literature summaries, qualitative interpretations, numerical outputs and proposed research gaps.
- Design a bounded research automation and use AI to support a grant application with appropriate human review.
- Explain how confidentiality, intellectual property, bias, reproducibility and disclosure affect their own use of AI.

:::

::: callout-questions

## ❓ Questions

1. Which tool or approach fits the research task, and what evidence will it actually see?
2. How can we move from a useful conversation to a workflow another researcher can check?
3. Where can AI assist interpretation, and which decisions require disciplinary judgement?
4. What would make an AI-assisted literature review, analysis or grant application defensible?

:::

## Structure & Agenda

This applied workshop builds on [Introduction to AI for Research](01-Introduction_to_AI_for_research.qmd) and [Prompting for Research](02-Prompting_for_research.qmd). It assumes familiarity with basic prompting and source checking; no programming background is required.

| Theme | Teaching | Activity and discussion |
|---|---|---|
| The current AI landscape | 15 minutes | 5 minutes |
| Effective research workflows | 10 minutes | 10 minutes |
| AI across the research lifecycle | 15 minutes | 10 minutes |
| AI for literature reviews | 15 minutes | 20 minutes |
| Qualitative and quantitative analysis | 15 minutes | 20 minutes |
| Agents and research automation | 10 minutes | 10 minutes |
| Grant applications | 5 minutes | 10 minutes |
| Research integrity and responsible use | 5 minutes | 5 minutes |

Allow **three hours of learning time**, plus breaks. The analysis activity offers two routes; choose one during the workshop and use the other for further practice. Sections can also be delivered as shorter linked sessions.

> 🔧 Leave with a tool choice, a checked evidence table, an analysis critique and a reusable workflow for one research task.

## Working Examples and Access

The running example is a proposed study of **peer writing groups for doctoral researchers**. The study extracts, interviews, dataset and funding call below are fictional teaching materials. They are not published evidence, real participant data or a live funding opportunity.

Use an institutionally approved AI service if available. Public tools mentioned here are examples, not a list of services approved by the University. Every exercise can also be completed through prompt design and manual critique without a paid account. For live literature practice, bring two or three papers that you are permitted to upload to the chosen service.

# The Current AI Landscape for Academic Research

## Models, Tools and Workflows

A **model** generates or interprets content. A **tool** gives you an interface, document access, search or code execution. A **workflow** organises these capabilities around a research task and its checks.

ChatGPT is one way to access AI. Other examples include [Claude](https://claude.com/product/overview), [Gemini](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/models) and [Microsoft Copilot Chat](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/copilot/overview). Model families include GPT, Claude, Gemini and [Mistral](https://docs.mistral.ai/models); a product may offer several models or choose between them automatically.

The same model can behave differently with a different document collection, search service or set of instructions. Record both the product and the model/version where the product exposes it.

> 🧭 Start with the task, the permitted inputs and the checks you can perform.

## Match the Tool to the Research Task

The following are starting points for evaluation, based on the providers' descriptions linked in the table. They are not comparative performance rankings. **Tool information checked: 14 September 2026.** Features, names, subscriptions and institutional access can change.

| Research task | Tools or approaches to consider | What needs checking |
|---|---|---|
| Refine a question, explain an idea or critique a draft | General assistants such as [Claude](https://claude.com/product/overview), Gemini or an approved Copilot service | Whether the response follows the supplied evidence and preserves disciplinary meaning |
| Explore a topic or locate public guidance | Web search with an assistant such as [Perplexity](https://www.perplexity.ai/help-center/en/articles/10352155-what-is-perplexity) | The original source, publication date and scope; web results include material beyond academic literature |
| Find papers using research questions | [Elicit](https://elicit.com/) or [Consensus](https://help.consensus.app/en/articles/9922660-how-to-search-best-practices), alongside disciplinary databases | Coverage, search filters, missed studies and whether answers use abstracts or full texts |
| Explore related papers and citation networks | [ResearchRabbit](https://www.researchrabbit.ai/) or [Litmaps](https://www.litmaps.com/) | Dependence on starting papers, indexing and citation patterns |
| Examine how a paper is cited | [Scite](https://scite.ai/) | The citing passage and study itself; citation classification is not a quality appraisal |
| Ask questions across a selected document collection | Google's [source notebooks](https://support.google.com/gemininotebook/answer/16206563?hl=en), known as NotebookLM and now described as Gemini Notebook in its help pages; approved document assistants | Which sources were included, which passages were retrieved and whether each citation supports the claim |
| Extract comparable fields across papers | [Elicit's extraction workflows](https://elicit.com/) or a structured prompt applied to approved PDFs | Field definitions, source locations, missing information and extraction errors |
| Work with interview text and coding | An approved assistant or [MAXQDA AI Assist](https://www.maxqda.com/products/ai-assist) | Data processing arrangements, exact quotations and fit with the analytical approach |
| Develop analysis code and visualisations | [GitHub Copilot](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/get-started/what-is-github-copilot) or an approved coding assistant, with R/Python and version control | Executed code, data transformations, statistical assumptions and reproducible results |

These categories overlap. Citation mapping, reference management and database searching remain valuable even when they do not use generative AI. Keep the reference library and analysis files in systems the research team can maintain.

## Choosing a Model or Mode

| Capability | When it may help | Practical limitation |
|---|---|---|
| Fast general text generation | Reformatting checked notes or suggesting alternative wording | Speed gives no assurance of factual accuracy |
| Reasoning-oriented mode | Comparing design options or working through a difficult coding problem | A persuasive explanation can still rest on incorrect assumptions |
| Long context or document retrieval | Working with protocols, theory texts or several papers | Accepted files may not be fully read or retrieved for every answer |
| Multimodal input | Discussing a figure, scanned page or image | Axes, mathematical notation, tables and OCR can be misread |
| Code execution | Calculating summaries and producing plots | An answer containing code does not prove that the code ran |
| Institutionally hosted open-weight models | Projects needing an approved, controlled computing environment | Hosting, hardware, licences, logs and external connections still need review |

Open weights mean model parameters are available under a licence; they do not automatically mean unrestricted use or local processing. Mistral, for example, documents both model options and their deployment characteristics in its [model catalogue](https://docs.mistral.ai/models). Check the exact model and service before making a data-handling decision.

## A Small Evaluation Beats a General Ranking

Compare candidate tools on the **same permitted material**. Include a straightforward case, an ambiguous case and a question the sources cannot answer.

- Can you trace claims to source passages or executed calculations?
- Does the tool preserve uncertainty, contrary evidence and missing values?
- Can you export the inputs, prompts, outputs and corrections?
- What are the total time, cost and checking effort?

> 🔎 Agreement between two AI tools is a reason to check the evidence, not independent confirmation of a finding.

::: callout-task

#### Task 1: Choose an Approach

::: panel-tabset

##### Exercise (3 minutes)

Choose an approach for each task and name one check:

1. Find newer papers related to a known article.
2. Compare the definitions of a concept in three approved PDFs.
3. Calculate changes in a dataset containing missing follow-up values.

##### Discussion (2 minutes)

Possible choices are citation exploration, a document assistant with source locations, and executable analysis code. Explain what the tool must have access to and what you would verify before reusing the result.

:::
:::

# Using AI Effectively in Research Workflows

## Build a Research Brief Before Prompting

The prompt pattern from [Prompting for Research](02-Prompting_for_research.qmd) becomes more useful when supported by a short research brief.

| Include | Example |
|---|---|
| Purpose and audience | Prepare a comparison for a doctoral supervision meeting |
| Research question and scope | How might peer writing groups support sustained writing over six weeks? |
| Definitions and analytical position | Distinguish writing time, confidence and completed outputs |
| Source list and versions | Teaching extracts A–C; no external sources for this task |
| Output and evidence requirements | One row per source; attach a source ID and location to each claim |
| Constraints | Do not infer causation, invent missing details or change the question |
| Acceptance checks | The researcher verifies every extracted value and claim |

Keep instructions separate from source text. Clearly label quotations, background notes and your own decisions so the assistant does not confuse them.

## Provide Documents Deliberately

1. Check permission to use each document in the selected service.
2. Give each source a stable ID and record its title, date and version.
3. Ask for a list of accessible sources and flag unreadable pages or tables.
4. Start with a small extraction task and check the result against the original.
5. Expand the task only when the source handling is adequate.

A URL in a prompt does not prove that the tool opened the page. A successful upload does not prove that a scanned table was read correctly. Ask for section headings, printed page numbers or passage locations; mark locations as unavailable when the tool cannot provide them reliably.

## Understand Retrieval and Context

**Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)** means retrieving source passages and supplying them to a model when it answers. This can make answers easier to trace, but the retrieval step may omit relevant evidence.

For a comparison across many papers, extract each paper into the same schema before asking for synthesis. Check individual rows before combining them. When a conversation becomes long or changes direction, start a new session with a checked brief and the current sources.

> 📄 A larger context window creates capacity for more material. It does not guarantee equal attention to every page.

## Work in Visible Stages

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[Define task and sources] --> B[Extract or draft]
    B --> C[Check against evidence]
    C --> D{Supported?}
    D -->|Revise| B
    D -->|Yes| E[Save output and decisions]
```

Ask the assistant to identify assumptions, unresolved questions and alternative interpretations. Then perform the checks yourself. Asking the same assistant to approve its answer can reveal weaknesses, but does not replace independent verification.

## A Reusable Research Prompt

```text
Task: Compare what sources A–C say about peer writing groups.
Context: I am preparing a research design discussion, not claiming an effect.
Sources: Use only the labelled teaching extracts supplied below.

First list the sources you can access and any missing information.
Then produce one row per source with:
source ID; design; participants; outcome or concept; finding;
source location; limitation; question requiring human review.

Distinguish reported findings from your interpretation.
Use "not reported" for missing details. Do not invent references or values.
Do not combine different outcomes into a single claim of effectiveness.
Finish with disagreements and uncertainties for me to check.
```

Replace the task and source IDs when reusing the template. Test the template again when the material, model or intended output changes.

::: callout-task

#### Task 2: Turn a Prompt into a Workflow

::: panel-tabset

##### Exercise (7 minutes)

Improve this request: *“Read these papers and tell me what my PhD should study.”*

Write a short research brief and three stages: extraction, comparison and researcher decision. Specify an output and a check for each stage. Include what should happen if a source is missing or the evidence conflicts.

##### Discussion (3 minutes)

Swap with a partner. Could they repeat the workflow using your instructions? Which stage requires a decision that the AI cannot make on your behalf?

:::
:::

# AI Across the Research Lifecycle

## Developing and Refining Research Questions

AI can help generate alternatives, expose ambiguous terms and check whether a question matches the proposed data. Supply your disciplinary context, practical constraints and the distinction between exploratory and confirmatory work.

**Broad starting point:** “Do writing groups work?”

**More focused alternatives:**

- How do doctoral researchers describe the role of peer writing groups in sustaining a writing routine?
- How does self-reported weekly writing time change during a six-week writing group?
- What study design could estimate the effect of a writing group compared with an appropriate alternative?

These questions need different evidence. The second describes change; it does not, by itself, establish that the group caused it.

> 📝 “Suggest three questions within this scope. For each, identify the construct, unit of analysis, feasible data and claims the design would not support. Label any proposed novelty as unverified.”

## Exploring Theory and Conceptual Frameworks

Use AI to compare **supplied theoretical texts**, clarify unfamiliar terms and identify tensions between explanations. Read the original theory and check how concepts are used in your discipline.

For the writing-group example, possible explanations might involve social accountability, protected time or confidence. These are candidate ideas for investigation. Ask for a table linking each proposed construct to a source, definition, possible observation and competing explanation.

An initial framework might propose:

**Group participation → protected writing time → a more regular writing routine**

Label each arrow as a proposed relationship. Add plausible contextual influences such as workload, caring responsibilities and supervisory support. A tidy diagram does not establish a mechanism or show that all relevant influences have been included.

## Identifying Research Gaps

AI can help organise possible gaps: an underrepresented population, a weakly measured construct, a conflicting result or an untested explanation. Each candidate needs checking.

| Proposed gap | Evidence needed before claiming it |
|---|---|
| “Nobody has studied this population” | Searches using alternative terms, relevant databases and citation trails |
| “Findings conflict” | Comparable outcomes, populations and methods; differences may explain the apparent conflict |
| “The mechanism is unknown” | Examination of theoretical and empirical work, including different disciplinary vocabularies |
| “A new method is needed” | A reason the method would answer a meaningful unresolved question |

Use *“not identified within these sources/searches”* when that is what you have established. A small collection or an empty search result cannot establish that no relevant research exists.

## Research Design, Interviews and Surveys

Ask AI to compare design options against the question, access, ethics, time and resources. Retain responsibility for sampling, measurement, power or sample adequacy, analysis and feasibility.

| Task | Useful AI support | Researcher responsibility |
|---|---|---|
| Research design | Compare interviews, observational follow-up and controlled evaluation | Choose an approach that can answer the question and justify its assumptions |
| Interview development | Draft open questions and optional probes | Avoid leading questions; consider power, distress, context and researcher position |
| Survey development | Flag double questions, unclear recall periods and response gaps | Select suitable measures, check permissions, pilot and assess validity |
| Analysis planning | List assumptions, required variables and possible failure points | Agree the plan and distinguish exploratory changes from planned analyses |

**Leading interview question:** “How did the helpful writing group improve your productivity?”

**A more open alternative:** “Tell me about your writing routine during the past six weeks.” Follow with “What, if anything, changed?” and “What else influenced that?”

For a survey, “The group improved my confidence and productivity” combines two constructs and presumes improvement. Separate the constructs and specify a time period. AI-generated items are drafts, not validated scales. Pilot them with appropriate people; simulated AI participants do not validate a questionnaire.

## Academic Writing and Critical Review

Start with your argument, verified evidence and target audience. Ask for an outline, unclear transitions, alternative wording or a structured critique. Compare revisions with the original for changes in meaning, certainty and attribution.

> 📝 “Review this draft against the supplied evidence table. Identify unsupported claims, causal language, missing counterarguments and unclear definitions. Return the original sentence, the issue and a suggested revision. Preserve citations and uncertainty; do not add references or results.”

Keep references in a reference manager and check them against the papers. A formatted bibliography can contain fabricated or irrelevant citations. Use AI critique on your own material only where permitted; externally assigned peer review has separate confidentiality and policy requirements.

::: callout-task

#### Task 3: Connect a Question to Evidence

::: panel-tabset

##### Exercise (7 minutes)

Choose one writing-group question above. Produce:

- one proposed explanation and an alternative explanation
- a suitable design and the evidence it would produce
- two open interview questions or two draft survey items
- one claim the design would not justify

Use AI if available, then revise at least one suggestion using your own judgement.

##### Discussion (3 minutes)

Explain why the data match the question. Identify one remaining issue for a supervisor, methods specialist or ethics review.

:::
:::

# AI for Literature Reviews

## Different Reviews Need Different Workflows

Exploring a topic, writing a narrative review and conducting a systematic review have different requirements. Decide the purpose, question and method before choosing a tool.

For a systematic or scoping review, work with an information specialist where possible. Define eligibility, sources, search strategy, screening and extraction procedures. Use reporting guidance appropriate to the review type: [PRISMA 2020](https://www.prisma-statement.org/prisma-2020) and relevant extensions support transparent reporting; they are not a guarantee that the review was conducted well.

An automatically generated “deep research” report can help orientation. Its label does not establish a reproducible search, complete coverage or a systematic review.

## Finding Papers and Exploring Citation Networks

1. Build concept blocks, synonyms and relevant subject headings. AI can propose terms; check them in the database's vocabulary.
2. Search suitable disciplinary databases, such as PubMed, Scopus or Web of Science where appropriate and available. Keep exact queries, database/platform names, dates and filters.
3. Use AI-assisted discovery to explore additional terminology and candidate papers. Record this as another search route.
4. Follow references backwards and citations forwards from several relevant starting papers, including contrary findings.
5. Export records to a reference manager. Check duplicates and distinguish multiple reports of one study from separate studies.

ResearchRabbit and Litmaps offer ways to explore connections and discover related work. Network recommendations depend on the indexed literature and your starting collection; less cited, recent, non-English or poorly indexed work can be missed. See the providers' descriptions of [ResearchRabbit](https://www.researchrabbit.ai/) and [Litmaps](https://www.litmaps.com/).

## Screening and Working Across PDFs

Define inclusion and exclusion criteria before screening. Pilot AI suggestions against a set reviewed by humans, including borderline cases and relevant studies that are easy to miss. Check excluded records as well as included ones; an attractive summary of the included set cannot reveal false exclusions.

For each PDF, retain a paper ID, bibliographic record and whether you have the full text, abstract only or a partial extract. Check supplements, tables, corrections and retractions where relevant. Keep screening decisions and reasons separate from extraction and interpretation.

Document how automation was used and validated. The [PRISMA expanded checklist](https://www.prisma-statement.org/s/PRISMA_2020_expanded_checklist-yc78.pdf) explicitly addresses reporting automation in selection and data collection. Follow the review protocol's requirements for human review and resolving disagreements.

## Extract First, Synthesise Second

Use a structured evidence matrix:

| Field | What to record |
|---|---|
| Identity | Paper ID, study ID, citation/DOI and source version |
| Design and setting | Method, population, recruitment, context and timing |
| Concepts and outcomes | Definitions, instruments, units and time points |
| Findings | Extracted result, uncertainty and the exact supporting location |
| Limitations | Reported limitations and your separate appraisal |
| Verification | Checked by whom, corrections and unresolved questions |

Do not let the assistant fill blanks with plausible values. Distinguish **not reported**, **not applicable** and **not accessible**. Reopen the paper when an extraction conflicts with another section or mixes up a group, unit or time point.

## Creating a Structured Literature Review

Once the matrix is checked, organise synthesis around research questions, themes, theories or methods. Compare what studies can tell you, where they differ and how much confidence their designs support.

A useful review structure is:

1. Question, scope and rationale.
2. Search, selection and appraisal approach.
3. Characteristics of the included evidence.
4. Synthesis of patterns, differences and competing explanations.
5. Limitations of both the evidence and the review process.
6. Implications and carefully bounded research gaps.

Ask AI to draft an outline from the checked matrix and attach paper IDs to each proposed claim. Then write and revise with the papers open. Avoid counting positive papers as proof of an effect; study quality, sample overlap, uncertainty and comparability matter. A meta-analysis requires a justified statistical method, not an average of AI summaries.

## Common Failure Modes

| Approach | Useful contribution | Risk to manage |
|---|---|---|
| Asking a chatbot from memory | Generate initial terms and questions | Invented papers, stale knowledge and unsupported novelty claims |
| Web-assisted answers | Find candidate sources quickly | Search ranking, weak sources and citations that do not support the adjacent claim |
| Scholarly AI search | Identify related papers using natural language | Uneven disciplinary coverage and opaque selection |
| Citation networks | Explore intellectual connections | Reinforcing the same well-cited cluster |
| Chatting with PDFs | Navigate and compare a defined collection | Retrieval omissions, OCR errors and confusion between papers |
| Automated synthesis | Draft a structure from extracted evidence | Flattening disagreements, mixing outcomes and hiding missing data |

> 📚 Verification has three parts: the source exists, the source says this, and the source supports this particular claim.

::: callout-task

#### Task 4: Build and Challenge an Evidence Matrix

::: panel-tabset

##### Teaching Sources

**These are fictional extracts, not references to real papers. Use their paragraph labels as source locations.**

**Source A, paragraph 1:** Twenty-four volunteers at one university joined a six-week peer writing group. Mean self-rated writing confidence was 12 before and 17 afterwards on a 0–20 scale. There was no comparison group. The extract does not report variation, follow-up response count or completed writing outputs.

**Source B, paragraph 1:** Interviews with eight group attendees described protected time and encouragement. Two interviewees said fixed meeting times conflicted with caring responsibilities. Non-attendees were not interviewed. Changes in writing output were not measured.

**Source C, paragraph 1:** A cross-sectional survey of 60 doctoral researchers compared people who chose to attend writing groups with non-attendees. Attendees reported more weekly writing time. The extract provides no group counts, numerical difference or adjustment for workload or motivation. Confidence was not measured.

##### Exercise (15 minutes)

Extract design, sample, outcome, finding, source location and limitations for A–C. Check every cell, then ask for a 100-word synthesis restricted to the extracts.

Challenge this proposed conclusion: *“Three studies prove that writing groups increase doctoral productivity, so universities should require attendance.”*

Identify at least three problems. Write a bounded synthesis and one question worth investigating. If using real papers instead, retain the same extraction and verification steps.

##### Discussion and Checks (5 minutes)

- A describes confidence, B describes experiences and C describes a cross-sectional association; these are different outcomes and designs.
- A lacks a comparator and important reporting details. C is vulnerable to differences between people who chose to attend and those who did not.
- B identifies both support and an access barrier; compulsory attendance is not justified.
- A defensible synthesis reports possible benefits and access issues while making clear that these extracts cannot establish a causal effect on productivity.

A question about flexible participation may be worth exploring. The extracts cannot establish that it is a gap in the wider literature.

:::
:::

# AI for Qualitative and Quantitative Data Analysis

## Begin with the Analysis Plan

AI can assist with organising material, drafting code and exploring interpretations. The research question and analytical approach determine what counts as a valid result.

Keep original data read-only, work on copies and preserve identifiers. Check what leaves your machine, including transcripts, prompts, file previews and error messages. For practice, use the synthetic examples below.

## Qualitative Analysis: Support at Different Stages

| Stage | Possible AI support | Essential human work |
|---|---|---|
| Transcription | Draft a transcript or flag unclear passages | Check consent, approved processing, speaker labels, omissions and relevant non-verbal context against recordings |
| Familiarisation | Locate passages or prepare navigational summaries | Read the material and write your own observations and reflexive notes |
| Initial coding | Suggest labels or apply a defined codebook to selected extracts | Check every retained assignment against the text and analytical purpose |
| Developing themes | Compare candidate patterns and retrieve contrasting passages | Develop and revise interpretations across the full dataset |
| Reporting | Organise checked extracts and critique an explanation | Preserve participants' meaning, anonymise appropriately and justify the interpretation |

For example, [MAXQDA AI Assist](https://www.maxqda.com/products/ai-assist) offers coding support, summaries and questions over text. Evaluate the feature's processing arrangements separately from those of the desktop software. A local project file does not mean an AI feature processes locally.

## Coding Is Not the Same as Thematic Analysis

Choose the approach before asking the model to “find themes”. In codebook-based work, provide definitions, inclusion/exclusion rules and examples. Pilot suggestions, retain disagreements and version codebook changes.

In **reflexive thematic analysis**, themes are developed through the researcher's situated interpretation and engagement with the data. Automated label agreement cannot establish the quality of that analysis. Braun and Clarke's [guidance on reflexive thematic analysis](https://www.thematicanalysis.net/doing-reflexive-ta/) explains this interpretative process; their [FAQs](https://www.thematicanalysis.net/faqs/) distinguish codes and themes.

Use AI suggestions, if methodologically appropriate, as material to interrogate. Keep a reflexive memo on how they influenced your attention. Seek exceptions, context and alternative readings; frequency alone does not determine a theme's significance.

## A Prompt for Inspectable Coding Suggestions

```text
Use only the labelled synthetic interview extracts below.
Suggest provisional descriptive codes about participation in writing groups.
Return: extract ID; exact quotation; proposed code; reason;
alternative interpretation; uncertainty or missing context.

Do not rewrite quotations or invent participants, experiences or motives.
Allow more than one code per extract and allow "unclear".
Look for evidence that complicates an initially positive interpretation.
These are coding suggestions for human review, not final themes.
```

Do not ask AI to generate participant quotations, fill gaps in interviews or claim saturation. Synthetic text can be useful for training, but must remain labelled and separate from empirical evidence.

## Quantitative Analysis: Keep the Computation Visible

Give the assistant a data dictionary, the study design, planned analysis and relevant software versions. Initially, a synthetic sample or schema may be enough to develop code without uploading real data.

Ask for a staged approach:

1. Validate column names, types, identifiers, units and allowed values.
2. Report missingness, duplicate keys and data problems before transformation.
3. Show the proposed analysis and assumptions for researcher review.
4. Generate code that preserves raw data and records any exclusions or derived variables.
5. Run the code in an approved environment and inspect its outputs.
6. Reproduce a small calculation independently and check the conclusions against the design.

Keep the script or notebook with its input version, package versions and random seeds where relevant. A chat message containing a result or a plausible library call is insufficient evidence that the calculation happened correctly.

## Statistical Support and Visualisation

| AI suggestion | Questions to ask before accepting it |
|---|---|
| “Run a t-test” | What is the estimand? Are observations paired, independent or clustered? What assumptions matter? |
| “Remove outliers” | Is there a documented data error or a scientifically justified rule? How would removal affect conclusions? |
| “Fill missing values with the mean” | Why are values missing? Is imputation justified by the analysis plan? How is uncertainty handled? |
| “This relationship is significant” | Did the test run? What are the effect size, interval, assumptions and multiple-testing implications? |
| “This predicts outcomes well” | Were training and evaluation data separated appropriately, including preprocessing and participant groups? |
| “Use a bar chart” | Would individual observations, distributions or paired changes answer the question more clearly? |

Ask AI to compare plausible methods and explain required information. Involve a statistician when the design or assumptions need specialist judgement. Do not select tests to achieve a preferred result or present exploratory findings as prespecified confirmation.

For figures, calculate from the actual data. Verify sample counts, labels, units, scales, uncertainty intervals and colour accessibility. Preserve the plotting code; a generated illustration is not a data visualisation unless its marks faithfully represent the data.

::: callout-task

#### Task 5: Check an AI-Assisted Analysis

Choose **one** route. Spend 15 minutes on the exercise and 5 minutes comparing checks with another group.

::: panel-tabset

##### Qualitative Route

These are synthetic extracts from three fictional interviewees:

- **I01, line 1:** “Booking the session made me protect the time. I did not always write more, but I stopped putting it off.”
- **I02, line 1:** “The others were encouraging. The afternoon slot clashed with collecting my children, so I only came twice.”
- **I03, line 1:** “I came most weeks. My supervisor's deadline was probably what got the chapter finished.”

Code the extracts yourself, then request suggestions using the prompt above. If working without AI, critique the proposed theme *“Writing groups cause higher productivity for everyone.”*

Keep, revise or reject each suggestion. Record one alternative explanation and one reflexive note about how your expectations influenced interpretation.

##### Quantitative Route

This synthetic dataset has **one row per person**. `participant_id` is a text identifier; `NA` means a missing value, not zero. Hours are self-reported writing time during the week before the group and during week six. These six fictional people are a separate practice dataset, not the participants described in Sources A–C.

```csv
participant_id,writing_hours_baseline,writing_hours_week6,sessions_attended
P001,4,6,6
P002,3,4,4
P003,5,NA,2
P004,2,2,5
P005,6,5,1
P006,4,4,3
```

Use this prompt, or work through the calculation manually:

```text
Use this synthetic dataset to describe within-person change in weekly
writing hours. Preserve all six rows and participant IDs in the source data.
First validate the schema and report missingness. Do not impute values.
Calculate week6 minus baseline only where both values are present.
Report the number of complete pairs and their mean change in hours/week.
Show individual paired values and propose a plot with labelled units.
If generating R or Python code, keep the raw data unchanged, report any
excluded observations for this calculation and explain each transformation.
Do not run a significance test or infer a causal effect.
```

Check the arithmetic by hand. If code is generated, review and run it in an approved environment; do not treat unexecuted output as a computed result.

##### Checks and Discussion

**Qualitative:** The extracts support possible interpretations involving protected time, encouragement, access barriers and an alternative influence from supervision. They do not establish universal benefit or causation. Any retained quotation must match its source exactly. Three teaching extracts are insufficient for a completed thematic analysis.

**Quantitative:** There are six unique IDs and one missing week-six value. The five complete changes are **2, 1, 0, −1 and 0 hours/week**, giving a mean change of **0.4 hours/week**. Report that P003 is unavailable for this paired calculation and retain their original record. A plot of paired observations can show the variation that the mean conceals. These data do not establish effectiveness.

**Both routes:** Identify an error that a fluent explanation could conceal. Record the specific check that would catch it.

:::
:::

# AI Agents and Research Automation

## From a Prompt to a Multi-Step Task

A saved prompt standardises an instruction. A **workflow** specifies a sequence of steps. An **agent** uses a model and tools to select or carry out steps towards a goal, potentially searching, reading files or running code.

Useful research candidates include preparing a draft digest from approved sources, extracting fields from permitted documents, checking metadata or assembling a report from validated analysis outputs. Begin with a manual workflow that works; test whether automation actually reduces total effort after checking.

| Repeated task | Support automation could provide | Human checkpoint |
|---|---|---|
| Literature monitoring | Retrieve new records, flag candidate duplicates and draft relevance notes | Confirm relevance and approve additions to the review library |
| Document extraction | Apply the same schema across approved papers | Check source locations, ambiguous fields and extraction failures |
| Analysis reporting | Run approved scripts and assemble tables and figures | Review logs, diagnostics and interpretation |
| Grant preparation | Compare a draft with a supplied call checklist | Confirm eligibility, commitments, costs and final content |

## Worked Example: A Literature Monitoring Assistant

Define the task as: **prepare a draft list of newly retrieved papers for review**.

1. Accept a checked search specification and the previous reviewed library.
2. Retrieve records from the approved database/API or process an exported search file.
3. Save query details, retrieval date and original record IDs.
4. Flag possible duplicates without deleting source records.
5. Add a provisional relevance note based on explicit criteria and accessible text.
6. Produce a draft table with source links, uncertainty and retrieval failures.
7. Stop for a researcher to decide which records to include.

The assistant must distinguish **zero results** from **a failed search**. Check coverage before assuming the literature has not changed. A saved prompt needs an enabled scheduler or automation platform to run periodically; it cannot monitor a topic merely because it says it will.

## Set Boundaries the System Can Enforce

Specify permitted sources, input folders, output locations and actions. Use read-only access where possible, a separate draft output area and a small trial batch. Set limits on run time, API requests, cost and retries, and stop with an explicit error when those limits are reached.

Web pages and PDFs can contain instructions that try to redirect an agent: **prompt injection**. Treat retrieved text as source material, not authority to change the task. A sentence in the prompt is only one defence; restrict tool permissions and review proposed actions as well.

> 🤖 Require human approval before sending messages, submitting applications, altering source data or making final screening and research decisions.

## A Reusable Agent Specification

```text
Purpose: Prepare a draft evidence-monitoring table for researcher review.
Input: Approved search export, eligibility criteria and previous library.
Permitted actions: Read these inputs; create a new draft table and run log.
Not permitted: Delete records, contact authors, upload other files,
change criteria, decide final inclusion or publish a report.

Output: Record ID; bibliographic details; candidate duplicate;
provisional relevance; supporting source; uncertainty; human decision field.
Stop if: An input is unreadable, a source is unavailable, permissions are
unclear or the configured run limits are reached. Report incomplete work.
Log: Date; tool/model; instruction version; input versions;
steps attempted; errors; checks actually performed; items awaiting review.
```

Test with a small known collection containing a duplicate, an irrelevant paper and an unreadable input. Review missed records and incorrect actions as well as correct output. When the model, sources or instructions change, repeat those checks.

::: callout-task

#### Task 6: Design a Bounded Research Automation

::: panel-tabset

##### Exercise (7 minutes)

Choose literature monitoring, extraction or analysis reporting. Adapt the specification above to define its inputs, actions, outputs, stop conditions and human checkpoint.

Add two test cases: one normal input and one failure such as an inaccessible paper or changed column name. State what you expect the system to do in each case.

##### Discussion (3 minutes)

Trace the task step by step. Where could a plausible but wrong result pass unnoticed? What permission or check would contain that failure?

:::
:::

# AI for Grant Applications

## Use the Funding Call as the Source

Provide the current call, eligibility rules, assessment criteria, word limits and an approved project brief. Ask AI to extract requirements before drafting prose. Record the call version and deadline, then verify them at the funder's original page.

| Application task | Useful AI support | What the team must supply or check |
|---|---|---|
| Assessing fit | Map the project to the call's priorities and eligibility criteria | Actual eligibility and strategic fit |
| Planning the application | Build a section checklist, timetable and evidence map | Owners, time available and internal submission deadlines |
| Drafting and editing | Structure the argument, clarify language and reduce word count | Original ideas, evidence, accurate claims and permitted use |
| Work packages and impact | Identify unclear dependencies, outputs and assumptions | Feasible methods, partner commitments and credible routes to benefit |
| Budget and resources | Check consistency between narrative and a supplied costing sheet | Approved rates, arithmetic, eligibility and research-office sign-off |
| Critical review | Identify weak links against the published criteria | Research quality and final submission decisions |

Do not invent preliminary findings, collaborators, letters of support, costs or promised outcomes. An AI-generated reviewer score is not a prediction of a funding decision.

## Applicant and Assessor Roles Have Different Rules

Under the [UKRI policy checked on 14 September 2026](https://www.ukri.org/publications/generative-artificial-intelligence-in-application-and-assessment-policy/use-of-generative-artificial-intelligence-in-application-preparation-and-assessment/), applicants are expected to be transparent about substantive AI use, while minimal language or formatting assistance need not be disclosed. Human involvement is required when developing applications or sections, and AI use during application interviews is prohibited.

UKRI assessors may use AI only for language refinement within the specified restrictions: application content and personal information must not be entered, and AI must not interpret or evaluate the application. Read the policy for the applicable role and check the particular funding opportunity before use. Other funders may set different conditions.

## A Prompt for Reviewing an Application Draft

```text
Use only the supplied fictional call and project notes.
Create a table: criterion; evidence already present; missing information;
question for the project team; proposed revision.
Quote or locate the relevant call requirement.

Do not invent findings, partnerships, commitments, costs or eligibility.
Flag conflicts between the work plan, proposed methods and resources.
Suggest revisions for human review; do not submit anything.
```

::: callout-task

#### Task 7: Review a Proposal Against a Call

::: panel-tabset

##### Fictional Call and Project

**Call, requirement 1:** Support a six-month pilot of an inclusive approach to doctoral researcher development.

**Call, requirement 2:** The application must specify its research question, recruitment approach, evaluation method, timetable and a justified budget of no more than £5,000.

**Project notes:** Pilot a flexible peer writing group. Recruit volunteers from one school, interview attendees and collect weekly writing-time diaries. The draft claims the study will prove increased productivity across the University. It proposes no approach to non-attendees, no timetable and an uncosted facilitator role. No partners have committed to the project.

##### Exercise (7 minutes)

Create a requirements matrix manually or with AI. Identify three missing or unsupported elements, revise the central claim and write two questions for the project team.

##### Discussion (3 minutes)

Check whether the method supports the intended conclusion and whether recruitment addresses inclusion. A stronger proposal would frame feasible pilot questions, supply a timetable and costed roles, and resolve participation barriers. AI cannot supply missing commitments or guarantee that the project meets the call.

:::
:::

# Research Integrity and Responsible Use of AI

## Confidentiality, Company Data and Intellectual Property

Before supplying material to a tool, check the data classification, ethics approval, participant information/consent, contracts and the institution's permitted processing arrangements. Removing names may not remove identifiable combinations of roles, events, locations or quotations.

Company datasets, partner documents, unpublished findings, patentable ideas and applications received in confidence require particular care. Access to a document is not automatically permission to upload it to another provider. Reading access to a paper also does not settle licence conditions for uploading or redistributing it.

Distinguish model training, retention, administrator access, hosting location, subprocessors and connector permissions. For example, Microsoft's [Copilot Chat privacy documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/copilot/privacy-and-protections) describes protections for work accounts while also explaining logging and separate handling of web search queries. A “not used for training” statement does not mean no data is stored or sent elsewhere.

If permission is unclear, use a synthetic example or a schema while seeking advice from the appropriate institutional data, research ethics, information security or contracts/IP team. Keep sensitive AI-use logs in approved storage too.

## Hallucinations, Bias and Appropriate Boundaries

| Risk | A practical response |
|---|---|
| Invented or distorted references | Verify title, authors, DOI and publication details, then read the passage supporting the claim |
| Unsupported interpretation | Separate source statements, calculations, researcher inference and AI suggestions |
| Bias in sources or output | Look for missing populations, languages, disciplines, contrary evidence and stereotyped interpretations |
| Overconfidence from fluent writing | Ask what evidence would overturn the claim and check it outside the conversation |
| Loss of context | Revisit complete papers, interviews and study designs before making conclusions |
| Fabricated evidence | Never present generated quotations, measurements, images or citations as observed research data |

AI can support accessibility and language clarity, but it can also standardise away a researcher's voice or a participant's meaning. Review what changed. A more polished answer is not necessarily a better account of the evidence.

## Reproducibility and a Useful Audit Trail

Record enough for a colleague to understand the contribution and reproduce the parts that can be reproduced:

```text
Date and researcher:
Task and reason for using AI:
Product, model/version if visible, account/service and relevant settings:
Input files, source IDs, versions and permission basis:
Prompt/template version and sequence of steps:
Original outputs, generated code and execution environment:
Checks performed, errors found and corrections:
Material retained, rejected or modified and by whom:
Remaining limitations and disclosure decision:
```

Model updates, changing search indexes and variable outputs can prevent identical reruns. Preserve the actual outputs and decisions rather than assuming a prompt alone is enough. Distinguish reproducible code execution from an AI conversation that can only be documented and evaluated.

## Disclosure, Authorship and Accountability

Authorship carries responsibility for the work; an AI system cannot take that responsibility. The researchers remain accountable for evidence, interpretation and the final text. [Springer Nature's guidance](https://group.springernature.com/gp/group/ai/ai-guidance-for-our-researchers-and-communities) emphasises human accountability and transparent use under its policies.

Check the current institution, funder and target journal requirements. Language editing, substantive drafting, analysis and research methods may require different descriptions. Disclosure does not make an otherwise prohibited or methodologically unsound use acceptable.

A disclosure should describe what actually happened, for example:

> “We used [tool and model/version, date] to suggest descriptive codes for approved transcript extracts. The research team checked each retained suggestion against the original text, revised the coding and developed the final interpretation. The input specification, prompts and decisions were retained in approved project storage.”

This is a template, not a declaration to copy regardless of your method. Replace the details and only claim checks that were performed.

::: callout-task

#### Task 8: Write Your Research AI Use Note

Choose one activity from this workshop. Spend three minutes recording the input, tool or manual approach, output, checks and decision. Then use two minutes to explain to a partner:

- one action you would permit in a real project
- one action that would need approval or specialist advice
- one decision that must remain with the research team

If no AI was used, record that and identify what would need to change before using the proposed workflow with real research material.

:::

# Further Information

::: callout-keypoints

## 📚 Key Points

- Choose tools by task, evidence access, data permissions and the ability to verify outputs.
- Use a research brief, labelled sources, structured outputs and visible checking stages.
- Develop questions, frameworks and instruments with disciplinary judgement; proposed novelty and validity need evidence.
- Build literature synthesis from verified records and extraction, preserving differences and uncertainty.
- Keep qualitative interpretation connected to the original material and numerical claims connected to executed analysis.
- Automate bounded steps with logs, failure handling and human checkpoints.
- Use AI to strengthen a grant application while retaining responsibility for its claims, commitments and compliance with the call.
- Record and disclose actual AI use according to the applicable requirements.

:::

::: callout-hints

## Further Practice and Guidance

- Revisit [Prompting for Research](02-Prompting_for_research.qmd) and the course [reference guide](../learners/reference.qmd) for prompt and validation habits.
- Use [Research Data Management](../../essential_digital_skills/episodes/04-research_data_managment.qmd) for organising, documenting and protecting project data.
- Build analysis skills through [Applied Data Science in Python](../../applied_python/index.qmd) or [Applied Data Science in R](../../applied_R/index.qmd).
- Read [PRISMA 2020](https://www.prisma-statement.org/prisma-2020) and its relevant extensions when planning review reporting.
- Consult [Braun and Clarke's thematic analysis resources](https://www.thematicanalysis.net/doing-reflexive-ta/) when considering methodological fit.
- Check the current [UKRI application and assessment policy](https://www.ukri.org/publications/generative-artificial-intelligence-in-application-and-assessment-policy/) and [Springer Nature guidance](https://group.springernature.com/gp/group/ai/ai-guidance-for-our-researchers-and-communities) alongside local requirements.
